---
title: "Logistic regression"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Logistic regression combines a Bernoulli response with the logit link. The SuperTelicity verb-type contrast has the specification stated below.

The Bernoulli likelihood is the joint probability of the fixed responses viewed as a function of the coefficients, and its product form uses the model's [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) assumption. A coefficient [standard error](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd) is the standard deviation of its estimator's sampling distribution, not response spread.

We first construct the Bernoulli likelihood, then fit and interpret the log-odds coefficient, and finally return predictions to the probability scale.

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),
\qquad
\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i.
$$

This model joins four earlier pieces: the [Bernoulli sampling model](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd), [odds and log odds](odds-and-log-odds.qmd), [maximum likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd), and [IRLS computation](iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd). Conditional on the predictors, the row likelihood and joint likelihood are

$$
p(y_i\mid\pi_i)=\pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i},
\qquad
L(\boldsymbol\beta;\mathbf y)=\prod_i
\pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i},
$$

where $\pi_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i)$. Before observing the data, $Y_i$ is random. After observation, $y_i$ is the fixed zero or one that enters this likelihood.

```{r}
#| label: fit-logistic-regression
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
st$verb_type <- factor(st$verb_type, levels = c("manner", "result"))
fit <- glm(prep_in ~ verb_type, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = st)
coef_table <- data.frame(term = names(coef(fit)), estimate = unname(coef(fit)),
                         odds_multiplier = exp(unname(coef(fit))))
coef_table
```

The intercept is the manner-verb log odds. The result coefficient is the result-minus-manner log odds difference, so

$$
e^{\beta_1}
=\frac{\pi_{\mathrm{result}}/(1-\pi_{\mathrm{result}})}
        {\pi_{\mathrm{manner}}/(1-\pi_{\mathrm{manner}})}.
$$

In this saturated two-group case, let $s_m/n_m$ and $s_r/n_r$ be the observed group proportions. Maximizing each group's binomial likelihood gives $\widehat\pi_m=s_m/n_m$ and $\widehat\pi_r=s_r/n_r$. Treatment coding thus yields

$$
\widehat\beta_0=\operatorname{logit}(s_m/n_m),
\qquad
\widehat\beta_1=\operatorname{logit}(s_r/n_r)-
\operatorname{logit}(s_m/n_m).
$$

```{r}
#| label: derive-two-group-logistic-coefficients
#| echo: true
group_counts <- aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st,
                          function(z) c(successes = sum(z), trials = length(z)))
manual <- with(group_counts,
  c(intercept = qlogis(prep_in[1, "successes"] / prep_in[1, "trials"]),
    result = qlogis(prep_in[2, "successes"] / prep_in[2, "trials"]) -
      qlogis(prep_in[1, "successes"] / prep_in[1, "trials"])))
rbind(manual = manual, glm = coef(fit))
```

The fitted coefficient is `r round(coef(fit)[[2L]], 3)` and its exponential is `r round(exp(coef(fit)[[2L]]), 3)`. The latter is an odds ratio, not a probability ratio.

```{r}
#| label: logistic-raw-and-fit
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
groups <- aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st, mean)
groups$fitted <- predict(fit, newdata = groups, type = "response")
plot_data <- rbind(transform(groups, value = prep_in, kind = "observed"),
                   transform(groups, value = fitted, kind = "fitted"))
ggplot(plot_data, aes(verb_type, value, shape = kind)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .18), size = 2.2) +
  labs(x = "Verb type", y = "Probability of an in-completion", shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

The two fitted probabilities equal the two observed proportions because this model has one parameter for each group mean. In richer models, interpret coefficients with response-scale predictions because the same log-odds change produces different probability changes at different baselines.

```{r}
#| label: same-logit-coefficient-different-baselines
#| echo: true
b <- unname(coef(fit)[[2L]])
baseline <- groups$prep_in
data.frame(baseline, after = plogis(qlogis(baseline) + b),
           change = plogis(qlogis(baseline) + b) - baseline)
```

This population model leaves participant and sentence deviations outside the likelihood so that the Bernoulli score equations remain visible. The SuperTelicity analysis uses a Bayesian logistic mixed model; repeated participants and sentences make the row-independent standard errors here unsuitable for confirmatory inference.

## Recap and check

1. Does $\exp(\beta_1)$ give a probability ratio? No. It gives an odds ratio.
2. Does a row-independent fit make repeated participants independent? No. The likelihood omits shared participant terms even though the same people contribute multiple rows, so its independence assumption remains a model limitation.

The [worked analysis](logistic-regression-example.qmd) next carries these mechanics through uncertainty and model checking.
